quiz.q: What's the key difference between how a function and a macro receive their arguments?
options: Functions receive values; macros receive tokens (code)
Macros receive values; functions receive tokens
Both receive fully evaluated values
There's no real difference
quiz.explain: A function operates on already-evaluated values at runtime. A macro receives the raw tokens of the call and expands into new code before type checking runs.

quiz.q: When does macro_rules! expansion happen relative to type checking?
options: Before type checking
After type checking
During type checking, interleaved
Only if compilation fails
quiz.explain: Macros expand fully into plain Rust source before the compiler starts checking types — a macro literally cannot see or reason about types.

quiz.q: In the pattern `($msg:expr)`, what does `:expr` do?
options: Declares $msg as a function parameter
A fragment specifier that limits $msg to matching an expression
Converts $msg into a string at compile time
Marks $msg as an optional argument
quiz.explain: Fragment specifiers like :expr, :ident, :ty constrain what shape of code a captured $name is allowed to match.

quiz.q: What does `$( $x:expr ),*` mean in a macro_rules! pattern?
options: Match exactly one expression
Match zero or more comma-separated expressions
Match a single block of code
Match a type name
quiz.explain: The $( ... ),* syntax captures a repeated, comma-separated list — the same mechanism vec! uses to accept any number of items.

quiz.q: Given `macro_rules! twice { ($x:expr) => { { $x; $x } }; }`, what does `twice!(n += 1)` do to `n`, starting from 0?
options: Increments n by 1, because $x is evaluated once and the result reused
Increments n by 2, because $x is pasted as raw tokens and both copies run
Leaves n at 0, because macros don't execute code
Fails to compile
quiz.explain: A macro copies tokens, not values. $x appears twice in the expansion, so `n += 1` literally runs twice, adding 2 total.

quiz.q: Why does `vec[1, 2, 3]` (without the `!`) fail to compile?
options: vec is a reserved keyword in Rust
The compiler looks for a function named vec, and none exists — only the vec! macro does
Square brackets are invalid syntax in Rust
vec! requires parentheses instead of brackets
quiz.explain: Without the !, Rust reads `vec[...]` as indexing into something named vec. No function or variable named vec exists — only the vec! macro.

quiz.q: A macro rule `($x:expr) => { ... }` is called as `my_vec![1, 2, 3]` and fails with 'no rules expected the token ,'. What's the fix?
options: Change :expr to :ty
Add repetition: `( $( $x:expr ),* )` in the pattern, and `$( ... )*` in the expansion
Remove the square brackets from the call site
Nothing — Rust automatically handles multiple arguments
quiz.explain: A single $x:expr pattern only matches one expression. Repetition syntax is required to accept a variable-length, comma-separated list.

quiz.q: Why should you generally prefer a plain function over a macro when both could work?
options: Functions always run faster at runtime
Macros are harder to read and debug and tooling understands them less well; reach for one only when a function truly can't do the job
Macros can't accept any arguments
Functions can't be unit tested
quiz.explain: Macros add real complexity — error messages point into the expansion, and editor tooling has weaker macro support. Use one only for variadic arguments or genuine code generation.

flashcards.back: That you're calling a macro, not a function. Macro calls always use `!`.

flashcards.front: When does a macro_rules! macro expand relative to type checking?
flashcards.back: Before type checking. Macros operate purely on tokens (syntax), so expansion happens first — the compiler only checks types on the code that comes out.
The `:type` part after a captured name in a macro pattern (e.g. `:expr`, `:ident`, `:ty`, `:block`) — it constrains what shape of code that capture is allowed to match.

flashcards.front: What does `$( $x:expr ),*` capture in a macro pattern?
flashcards.back: Zero or more expressions, separated by commas — the mechanism behind variadic macros like `vec!`.

flashcards.front: If `$x` appears twice in a macro's expansion and the caller passes `n += 1`, what happens when the macro runs?
flashcards.back: `n += 1` runs twice — macros paste raw tokens, not evaluated values, so repeating `$x` repeats the code.

flashcards.front: When should you reach for a macro instead of a function?
flashcards.back: Only when a function genuinely can't do the job — a variable number of arguments, or generating new code (structs, impls, match arms) that a function can't produce.

flashcards.front: What's the basic shape of a macro_rules! definition?
flashcards.back: `macro_rules! name { (pattern) => { expansion }; }` — the pattern captures pieces of the call, the expansion is the code generated in their place.
